To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) MVs isolated from cancer cells contain unique cargo that can be used as a diagnostic marker for cancer and (ii) MVs isolated form cancer cells can promote the survival and proliferation of non-transformed cells, which may help cancer cells survive in the tumor microenvironment and metastasize to distant sites.
oncogenic transformation gives MVs a unique cargo, which is a signaling protein kinase, that promotes their ability to induce transformed phenotypes in recipient normal cells.

the induction of cellular transformation leads to a unique set of signaling proteins being packaged into microvesicles (EVs) that can be transferred to other cells and promote their survival and growth under conditions that promote the transformed phenotype.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the biogenesis, composition, and functional significance of MVs and exosomes in cancer.
the role of extracellular vesicles (exosomes and microvesicules) in intercellular communication.
the role that extracellular vesicles (EVs) play in cancer progression.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the oncogenic transformation of cells gives rise to a novel class of microvesicles that are capable of transferring a unique set of signaling proteins to non-transformed cells, thereby inducing their transformation.
the presence of focal adhesion kinase in MVs from onco-Dlb transformed cells can be used as a biomarker for the presence of cancer cells in a patient.
the induction of cellular transformation gives rise to microvesicles, which uniquely contain the signaling protein kinase, Focal adhesion kinase.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the induction of cellular transformation leads to the production of MVs that contain a unique signaling tyrosine kinase, which can be transferred between cells and promote the transformed phenotype.
the oncogene Dbl induces the release of MVs from fibroblasts, which contain the protein FAK.

we have identified a unique signaling protein that is present in MVs isolated from cancer cells, and that this protein can induce the transformed phenotype when added to normal cells, thus offering a novel mechanism for intercellular communication and cancer progression.
The main takeaway from our work is that

oncogenic transformation of cells leads to the generation of MVs, which contain a unique set of signaling proteins, including a kinase that can be transferred to normal cells and promote the transformed phenotype.
the oncogenic transformation of a cell can change the cargo of its MVs, leading to the secretion of signaling proteins and RNAs that promote cancer cell survival and proliferation.
MVs can be used as a diagnostic marker for malignant disease.
